entities.name: Caelestius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Caelestius (b. c. 380 CE, Campania; d. after 418 CE, possibly 500 CE), a Roman lawyer turned ascetic and theologian, emerged as Pelagius's most vocal and systematic disciple, profoundly shaping the Pelagian controversy during the early 5th century. His rigorous articulation of human free will and denial of original sin, particularly his assertion that Adam's sin harmed only himself and that infants are born without sin, directly challenged the nascent Augustinian doctrine of grace, setting the stage for one of late antiquity's most enduring theological disputes. Operating primarily in Rome, Carthage, and Ephesus, Caelestius was instrumental in disseminating Pelagian ideas across the Western Roman Empire, forcing the Church to define its stance on fundamental questions of human nature and divine intervention.

Caelestius's active period began around 405 CE in Rome, where he met Pelagius. After the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410 CE, he traveled to Carthage, seeking ordination as a presbyter. His application was rejected in 411 CE by a synod presided over by Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, due to charges of heresy brought by Paulinus of Milan, who presented six specific propositions attributed to Caelestius, including the claim that Adam's sin did not transmit to his progeny and that infants are born in the same state as Adam before the fall. This condemnation marked the first official ecclesiastical censure of Pelagian tenets. Subsequently, Caelestius continued to defend his views in Ephesus, where he was ordained, and later in Constantinople, before appealing to Pope Zosimus in Rome in 417 CE, momentarily achieving a reprieve before a definitive condemnation by the Council of Carthage in 418 CE and the Imperial Edict of Honorius.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Caelestius's systematic articulation of Pelagianism forced the early Church to define its core doctrines on grace and original sin, directly influencing the theological development of Augustine of Hippo and shaping the trajectory of Western Christian thought for centuries.
